meaningMnemonic: This looks like the west radical with a little something extra under it… And if you ask for "a little something extra" in the Wild West, you're going to get a big ol' decanter of bourbon, moonshine, or some other kind of very strong alcohol — which happens to be exactly what this radical looks like! That extra line at the bottom is just the little bit of alcohol still left in the bottle.

This radical has a bean (the square in the middle) between the ground and some roots. That bean is going to turn into a plant someday. What will that plant produce? Great big beans , like the ones from Jack and the Beanstalk.

This looks like a tree with something tied around its middle, holding it tight. If you untied that middle part you'd realize it's actually a bunch of little trees (aka twigs and sticks) tied in a bundle !

This is the Chinese radical. Why? Because it looks like a traditional Chinese pagoda! One of those towers with a bunch of tiered roofs, you know? Sure, lots of Asian countries have pagodas, but let's be honest — the Chinese probably came up with them first.
Doesn't this radical look like one of those old-fashioned dynamite plunger things that gets pushed to set the fuse? That makes this dynamite!

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means fault . Just in case you don't remember the kanji's meaning mnemonic, here's the gist: That slide is your husband's only fault . He spends all day sliding down it like a madman, which is why his hair sticks straight up on top. Maybe that's another fault… It's also a way to remember this is 失 (fault), not 矢 (arrow).

A leaf-shaped protrusion coming out of a shellfish. What is it? The mysterious geoduck ! The geoduck is a giant clam so big that most of it grows outside its shell. If you've never seen a geoduck, look it up now. You'll never be able to unsee it.

In winter, your mouth longs for a kiss . You know, because your lips get cold and you want someone to warm them up. How do you think that whole mistletoe thing got started? Cold winter mouths, longing for a kiss. So just imagine the top part of this radical as some winter mistletoe (or holly leaves, since that's probably easier), and the bottom part as a kissy mouth.
If you kick a cliff twice you'll start a landslide ! Oh no!

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means music ! 曲 even looks like a musical score with two notes in the middle. Huh? Real sheet music has more lines, you say? Hey, it's a radical — we're saving ink, not performing Beethoven here. Alternatively, you could use the kanji mnemonic you learned: There are twenty mouths singing beautiful music together.
This is the pope radical. Why? Because it looks like a pope hat! This one's got a big old cross on top, and it can only be worn by the pope.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means sell . Just in case you don't remember, here's the kanji meaning mnemonic: A samurai has come bearing foreheads and legs that he's trying to sell . He thought it was a waste to leave all his slain enemies on the battlefield, so he gathered up their foreheads and legs to sell on the black market for some extra cash. Hey, no judging! A samurai's gotta sell what a samurai's gotta sell, okay?

This is the canopy radical with ice running down the back. If you hang out in a cold canopy like this you'll definitely get sick . Imagine being sick and alone inside a cold canopy. Brrrr, oh no... ACHOO!

This radical looks like a little flight of stairs , don't you think? Also note it's being held up by a pillar or beam or something on the left side. After all, you don't want your stairs collapsing as you walk up them.

Oh no, you let the pope's hat get snatched by a lion! You get it back, but it's all crooked, so you've got to make it straight again. The pope needs a straight, dignified hat, so you'd better straighten that thing out.
There is a stool sticking out of the dirt. You walk up and realize it has writing on it. It's actually a tombstone . You can sit on it and remember the people who are below the dirt now.
This is the turkey radical. It kinda looks like a turkey facing to the left, with big tail feathers fanning out behind it. See it? You can practically hear this thing gobble!

You give your scooter to a turkey so that it can advance . The turkey was trying and failing to walk through a crowded street, so out of the goodness of your heart you gave it a scooter so it could advance. Hints Imagine picking up the turkey and putting it on your scooter. Of course, you give it your helmet as well, safety first.
readingMnemonic: You wave as the turkey advance s into the street at top speeds, collides with a car, and scrapes up its shin s ( しん ) almost immediately. Ah! Hints Silly turkey, you can't advance that fast, of course you'll hurt your shins. It's better to advance slowly, but I guess I couldn't expect you to know that.

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami is an alcohol ic beverage containing a lot of alcohol . It’s 3 different kinds of rums, pineapple juice, and grenadine. It’ll hit you like a tsunami though. This alcoholic drink has a kick to it. Hints It’s made with spiced rum, coconut rum, and dark rum. Imagine yourself on a sandy beach drinking this cocktail. Feel the sun on your face and the wind in your hair as you sip on this fruity and rummy alcoholic beverage known as a tsunami. You could even picture an actual tsunami in the water coming right for you. I wouldn’t recommend it though—actual tsunami are scary, not drinkable and delicious.
readingMnemonic: As you lie on this beach, the alcohol keeps coming down a chu te ( しゅ ), straight into your mouth. You can feel the sand in your toes and the alcohol sliding down your throat from this special tsunami chute. Hints Picture the alcohol flowing down this long chute from somewhere far away. You try to see where it's coming from, but all you can see is this long, long chute stretching along the entire beach, until it disappears into the distance. You should probably be concerned that you're nonstop drinking alcohol from a random chute, but it tastes so good!

meaningMnemonic: If you give a woman a machine she'll begin learning how to use it right away. She'll also get it to start before anyone else could. Women are really good at starting up new machines! Hints Picture a woman seeing a new machine and beginning work on it right away to see how she can start it up.
readingMnemonic: Actually, before she can begin , she has to shear the shee p ( し ) over there. The machine is going to turn wool into yarn, but you can't just start that process by shoving the sheep in there. You have to keep the little sheep safe! Hints Picture a machine starting up as the woman begins to shear the sheep. Picture the sheep staring at you, staring at it.

meaningMnemonic: You have spikes growing out of a sheep with fins . Turn this thing into a business ! You could totally charge people money to look at it. Sure, you could also donate it to science, but a business-minded person like you knows a business opportunity when you see one. Step right up! Just five dollars for a glance at the rare spiky mer-sheep! Hints Imagine all the money you'll rake in with this new business. People will come from far and wide to see the spiky mer-sheep sideshow. And for an extra charge you'll let 'em touch those pointy spikes and slimy fins. Oh yes, business will be booming.
readingMnemonic: As you evolve your business , you let customers feed the sheep gyo za ( ぎょう ) dumplings, its favorite snack. For a nominal fee, of course. People love it when the mutant sheep eats gyoza out of their hands. Wouldn't you? Hints Imagine the smell of garlicky gyoza filling the sideshow tent, as customers try to feed the sheep and compete for its attention. Business is so good that the sheep gets tired of gyoza and won't eat it anymore. Oh well… Skewer them on its spikes and save 'em for later.

meaningMnemonic: If someone sticks bamboo in your eye twenty times, the first thing your brain does is calculate how painful it is. Your brain's pain calculation will determine how you calculate your next move. Hints Your next move is to go to the doctor, because your brain has calculated that the pain is extreme. Imagine the doctor asking how much it hurts. Well, on a scale of one to ten, doctor, I'd calculate this is about a twenty.
readingMnemonic: Next you want to calculate how much punishment your bamboo attacker deserves, so you call on San ta-san ( さん ). Santa-san is always calculating how many pieces of coal the naughty children deserve, so he's perfect for this calculation job. Hints Imagine trekking through the frozen wastes of the North Pole (with your eye patch on) to obtain Santa-san's calculation advice. After much discussion, he concludes that your bamboo attacker deserves twenty. No, not twenty years in prison — just twenty pieces of coal. Oh, how disappointing…

meaningMnemonic: While riding your scooter , you bang your forehead on the car in front. Your scooter's wrecked, so you have to carry it home. You'll need a lot of luck to get that scooter home safely. Hints Imagine trying to carry your scooter down a busy road, with all the cars whizzing past. Your forehead is still hurting from that nasty bang. Good luck!
readingMnemonic: As you carry the scooter, your luck turns, and it starts to rain, so you pull out your um brella ( うん ). Now you're holding your scooter, your forehead, and an umbrella. Hints It's hard enough to carry a scooter in heavy traffic, but now you have to try to keep yourself and it dry with an umbrella too.

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami hit ancient China and formed the Chinese country we know now as... China ! Sometimes this kanji also means man . In fact, it used to refer specifically to people of the Han dynasty, but over time evolved into a term for men in specific contexts. Hints Picture the world way far away, from space. You see a giant tsunami carve out a massive chunk of land to the west of Japan on the main continent. Slowly the tsunami waters recede, leaving the outline of China.
readingMnemonic: You peer closer at China and see one man, Genghis Khan ( かん ), leading his troops into the vast country, ready to conquer all the Chinese people living in China! Hints Khan is only one man, but watch as he takes China for himself. A tiny little flag with a horse on it is raised in the middle, for all of the Chinese people to see. Hmm, this could be a problem.

meaningMnemonic: When the mouth of a bird opens, you're most likely to hear a chirp . This is how birds communicate. They open their mouths and let out a series of chirps. Chirp chirp chirp! Hints Imagine yourself out in the wilderness on a sunny day. The weather is perfect and the scenery is beautiful. The only sound you can hear is the chirp of birds throughout the woods around you. It's very peaceful.
readingMnemonic: The best way to experience the chirp -chirping of birds is to offer them na chos ( な ). Birds love nachos so much, it's a guaranteed way to make them chirp with delight. Hints Picture yourself surrounded by birds of all kinds, handing out nachos. Just listen to their happy chirping. They're sitting on your arms, shoulders, and even your head, trying to get closer to the nachos. That chirping is so loud!

meaningMnemonic: You chase a turkey up a tree to collect it. At least, you will once you've gather ed enough turkeys into this one tree. Hints Collect another turkey, send it flying and gobbling up into the tree next to the other one.
readingMnemonic: Once you've collect ed enough turkeys, you're going to turn them into a shoe ( しゅう ). Maybe even two shoes, but that will mean gather ing even more turkeys! Hints Picture the nice, feathered shoes you'll be able to make once you've gathered all of these turkeys together. Ohoho, you can't wait! Go collect another turkey!

meaningMnemonic: You don't want to keep all the alcohol to yourself ( oneself ), so you distribute it to all of your friends. Heck, not just your friends, to everyone you can find! Hints Don't be that person who keeps the alcohol all to themselves. Distribute it to all of the legally-aged people you know!
readingMnemonic: As you distribute the alcohol you say a hai ku ( はい ): Here you go my friends Alcohol for everyone Never drink alone Hints This becomes the haiku you say before every party, every potluck, and every night out at the bar. You even get it tattoo'd to your arm.

meaningMnemonic: You can eat all you want, but you'll still lack something to drink . You can't live just from eating, you have to drink things too! Hints Imagine eating and eating and lacking a delicious, cold, thirst-quenching drink. Your mouth is dry. You have to drink something, anything!
readingMnemonic: You get desperate for a drink and put some no ri ( の ) seaweed in a blender, trying to create a drink of your own. Hints Luckily, this nori isn't dried and pressed like they usually are, and you manage to make a bright green nori drink. You gulp it down, and even though it tastes like the ocean, it hits the spot!

meaningMnemonic: The thread of winter and ice has brought this year to its end . Once you're in the long thread of winter and ice, you know the year will end soon. Hints Picture the season of winter as a long thread, embalmed in ice. At the end of it is the year’s end. The thread of winter and ice brings you closure, it marks the end.
readingMnemonic: Whenever winter end s, you take the thread covered in ice, and lace it into your shoe ( しゅう ). Hints This thread isn't just a metaphor, it's real! Feel the cold ice on it, as you lace it into your shoe. An age old tradition, the lacing of icy threads as winter ends. Your shoes will look so cool, or should I say… iced out.

meaningMnemonic: You stand on a cliff , a hair 's breadth away from the edge, when out of nowhere a geoduck slaps you in the face . The force makes you back away from the edge of the cliff, and your face is all slimy from the geoduck's residue. Hints Imagine being slapped in the face with a geoduck — a sharp hot pain, which then mingles with the cold geoduck residue left behind on your face. It's a strange, contradictory sensation.
readingMnemonic: But where did that geoduck come from? As you turn from the cliff edge, you find yourself face -to-face with a cow ( かお ). This cow is the one who hit you in the face with a geoduck. You don't know why, but something about your face has upset the cow. Hints Cows are big animals. So you probably got hit in the face with that geoduck pretty hard. Imagine the lingering pain, and how indignant you'd feel. Imagine getting in that cow's face and demanding an explanation.

meaningMnemonic: Flowers are knocked down by a violent tsunami , and swirl through the air to kiss your face gently as they fall . With the tsunami came a great windy storm that blew the flowers down. Amongst all the destruction, it's a pretty sight to watch them fall. Hints Imagine being out in this tsunami-induced storm. You're wet, cold, and scared, but you're calmed and mesmerized by how the flowers dance in the wind before they finally fall.
readingMnemonic: You want to save these flowers that fall around you, so you take out a drying rack ( らく ) and place them carefully on it. Any flowers that fall will go on the rack like this, so can save them for later. Hints Imagine running around catching the flowers as they fall. Imagine placing each fallen petal onto the rack to keep it safe and dry.

meaningMnemonic: You blast your music loud so it causes a landslide , revealing the perfect soil for farming ! Musically moved dirt is perfect for agriculture . Hints Imagine slowly turning up your big boombox until your ears hurt and the ground beneath your feet is vibrating with the beat. Soon you and the boombox are sliding with all of the earth down the hill and onto your farmland. Hooray, now the farming can begin!
readingMnemonic: The first person to come up with this farming method was No stradamus ( のう ), the famous seer and prophecy man. He predicted humans of the future would use special "yell cubes" to "move that good earth." Hints Picture Nostradamus flailing his arms and trying to explain his vision to the farmers at the time. He knows that if they listen their farming techniques will improve, but they're looking at him like he's nuts.

meaningMnemonic: You jump on your scooter with a big bundle to go as fast as you can! You have a bundle of pizzas in here, and they need to be delivered as fast as you can get them there! Hints Imagine how fast you can go on your scooter holding this bundle. It's way faster than trying to go on foot, that's for sure!
readingMnemonic: You were going so fast , you only put on sock s ( そく ). So now you're barreling down the street at top speeds in just your sad, white socks. Hints Imagine riding the scooter as fast as you can in just your socks. You can feel the wind pulling them off your feet!

meaningMnemonic: Think about it this way. There is a famous fishing lure inventor, working on his best work ever. He’s old, and he’s been trying to make the best fishing lure for the last 50 years, and knows this will be his last invention. Then he figures it out. He takes one barb , and connects the end of it to the top of another barb . When he does this, he knows his work is finally finish ed. Hints Make sure you look at this amazing fishing lure too - hold it in your hand, see the two barbs fused together. Think about how strange this lure is. Is this really the best in the world? Will this really finish all other fishing lures?
readingMnemonic: How does the fish lure maker test his newly finish ed lure out? The one he just finished? He gets in a row ( りょう ) boat and rows out into the sea. Hints Make him think that he can’t just use his new lure on the side of the lake / ocean / whatever. He has to get out there, but unfortunately all he has is a crappy row boat. Imagine the row boat being terrible, leaky, and dangerous, which is why you’re surprised when he goes for it. That’s a terrible row boat to use! If you do this, you'll focus your mind on the rowboat part of things, which will help you to remember the reading of this kanji.

meaningMnemonic: If you feed a lot of beans to a geoduck , its head will grow larger. To a geoduck, beans are a brain food, so by eating beans, it can grow an incredibly large head. Geoducks already look strange enough as it is, let alone with engorged heads. Hints Imagine, if you will, a geoduck. Now imagine it with a massive head. It looks ridiculous, and more disgusting than ever. It's actually really creeping you out, because the head keeps getting larger as the geoduck eats more beans. Ew.
readingMnemonic: As the geoduck eats more and more beans its head gets bigger and bigger, until finally the head explodes like an atomi c ( あたま ) bomb. BOOM! Geoduck parts go flying everywhere and pieces of its massive head float to the ground as atomic fallout. Hints Remember how gross geoducks are? Of course you do. Now imagine one exploding its atomic head right in front of you. You've got geoduck mess all over yourself. It's gross, slimy, sticky, and covering you from head to toe. It's wretched.

meaningMnemonic: If you go up to a gate and press your ear to it, you'll hear what's going on on the other side. The people on the other side will have no idea you can hear their conversation. Hints I'm sure you've pressed your ear up against a wall, door, or gate before to hear what's going on on the other side. Remember back to a time you did this and how sneaky you felt listening in on people without them knowing. You sneaky frood, you.
readingMnemonic: From the other side of the gate, you hear one of the people start to play a song on a recorder. You recognize the song as "Hot Cross Bun s ( ぶん )." You haven't heard this song since grade school. "Hot cross buns, hot cross buns~" Hints I'm sure many of you were forced to play "Hot Cross Buns" on the recorder in school at some point. Picture yourself playing this song and remember the melody when you see this kanji.

meaningMnemonic: This building has a roof and will teach you about the origin of many things. It's an institution ! Hints Institutions are places of learning, but they have to be a physical place with a roof and all that. If you're learning out in a field somewhere, that's probably not a proper institution.
readingMnemonic: What does institution start with? In ( いん )! Hints Just remember, it's an IN-stitution, and you'll know this reading easy-peasy.

meaningMnemonic: You say something about the circumference of this area. You've looked around this whole area, making a big circle around it, because you are trying to investigate something that happened here. You also say this thing in a really quiet tone of voice, because you don't want the person or thing you're investigating to know you're on to them. Hints Because the radical circumference is in play, you can think of the crime scene you're investigating as a statue of a giant globe, and you're doing a circumference around it. Then, in the reading, we'll think about what you'll say .
readingMnemonic: "I came here to investigate this place, and I did indeed find out who the criminal is... it's none other than Mrs. Chou ( ちょう )!" Hints From what you know about evil Mrs. Chou, you probably could have guessed it was her. The "Circumference Investigation" is now over, though you do still have to catch the perp, Mrs. Chou.

meaningMnemonic: You look at some gold and notice a fault in it. You scrape at the fault and see that it's just sprayed with gold paint. It's not gold, it's (comparatively) worthless iron ! Hints You think you've found a ton of gold bars! Imagine being so happy about this. Then, imagine your heart dropping in your chest when you notice the fault. Then, it dropping down even farther when you figure out it's merely iron.
readingMnemonic: Do you know that movie, Tetsu o ( てつ ) the Iron Man? We talked about it on Tofugu a while back. It’s one of the wackiest Japanese movies of all time. If you don’t know about Tetsuo the Iron Man, you should definitely look it up (if you aren't averse to horror/violent films). Tetsuo is one of the most insane movies in the history of ever. Hints Watch a trailer on YouTube for Tetsuo the Iron Man. Go ahead, do it now – I’ll wait. Did you watch it? Remember that nonsense every time you see this kanji.

meaningMnemonic: What you say between five mouth s is a language . As long as there are five different people saying these same words with their five mouths, it's considered its own language. Hints Picture these five mouths saying the same language to each other. They can understand each other! The mouths are smiling and laughing too.
readingMnemonic: Another mouth joins in speaking the language , but it's green and scaled and... it's Go dzilla's ( ご ) mouth! Godzilla speaks this language too. Hints Godzilla speaks a language some people understand! You wish you knew this earlier, then you might have been able to stop some of his destruction. Try to say, "Hey Godzilla, please stop destroying my city," in his language. It's a lot of growling and yelling. He doesn't seem to understand you. You better practice your pronunciation.

meaningMnemonic: All the flowers in the world of tree s owe their existence to the humble leaf . That's because leaves are how trees, and therefore flowers, get their nutrients from the sun. Hints Leaves, no matter how little, are the most important thing in the world for trees and flowers.
readingMnemonic: Picture a little flower working really hard to grow its first leaf. The leaf pops out and it shouts, " Hah ( は )!” Hints は is the sound of a leaf coming into existence. Whenever you see a plant from now on, hear the little "hah!" sound it makes when each leaf pops out of its body.

meaningMnemonic: You find some feathers that are so perfectly white , you want to learn more about where they came from and what they're made of. Hints Picture yourself in a library poring through huge tomes on feathers, specifically for completely white ones. You want to learn everything you can!
readingMnemonic: You learn that you should tie these white feathers to your shoe s ( しゅう ). You do it before you learn what it will do, and then suddenly you're jump-flying out of the building. Hints Oh geez, oh no. You better learn how to control these shoes before you—CRASH!!! Welp, you just shot through a plane. You need to learn more before you act next time.

meaningMnemonic: For a car , a tombstone is lightweight . Cars are very strong, you see, so something heavy like a tombstone is no match for them. All cars find tombstones to be light and easy to transport. Hints Picture yourself trying to move a huge slab tombstone. It’s difficult, no? I bet you wish you had a car or some other vehicle to make the process much less painful. Your arms are getting sore from carrying the tombstone and you’re getting sweaty and hot from all the work. What you would do for a car with air conditioning.
readingMnemonic: What do you wish you had to transport this tombstone? Oh, that’s right, a car. So you need some kind of car loo phole ( かる ). If you had a car, this tombstone moving business would be no problem. To cars, tombstones are naught but lightweight pebbles! But the rules say you can't use cars to carry tombstones, so you need to find a car loophole. Hints Remember all that hard work you were doing before and how you got all sweaty and gross? Now imagine yourself inside of a nice car with air conditioning, and the tombstone in the trunk. It feels great doesn’t it? The air conditioning is perfect, and driving a car is much easier than carrying a tombstone around. Thank goodness you found a car loophole in the tombstone carrying rules.

meaningMnemonic: You can use a long piece of thread during white water rafting as a safety line . Sure it's thin, but if someone goes overboard even a line of thread is better than nothing. Throw them a line and drag them back aboard! Hints Imagine you're the person who fell overboard. The white water is rushing violently and it is deathly cold. Feel the water and freezing temperature on your skin. But look! Someone has thrown you a line of thread! You're saved!
readingMnemonic: The person who threw you that line of thread is actually a cen taur ( せん ). How kind of him. After you are safe you hop on the centaur's back and ride around to get the wind to dry you off. Hints Coming out of the rushing water, this centaur is like an angel sent from heaven. He's just saved your life. Imagine the happiness and gratitude you feel towards this centaur as you are pulled to safety by that line of thread.

meaningMnemonic: Let the sun shine into your ear while sitting on a stool and make sure most of it gets in your head. You want to fill your brain with the most sun anyone ever has. Hints Most of the sun is getting into your ear, but not all of it. Darn, maybe you should try angling yourself a different way.
readingMnemonic: Most of this is for your cy borg ( さい ). You're testing out a new way to power it, but if you can't get most of the sun into your ear, it won't be enough to power most of the cyborg's robo-parts. Hints Install the part into your cyborg. As long as most of the sun gets into its human ear, most of its cyborg bits will have power.

meaningMnemonic: A gate with a lantern is open for you. That's convenient, since it's pretty dark out and you might not have seen the open gate without the lantern's help. Hints Imagine being a traveler, walking around the outside of a huge walled city. You really need to get inside but all of the gates are closed. Finally, you see a single, bright lantern marking the open gate! What a relief.
readingMnemonic: This open gate is in the water though, so you'll need a kay ak ( かい ) to get in. Luckily, you've been carrying your kayak with you just in case. Hints Imagine kayaking in the dark toward an open gate. Finally, you've made it!

meaningMnemonic: Did you know that those strange geoduck creatures were once used to make page s? Okay maybe not, but it makes for a memorable image! Hints Imagine the strange, gooey books you'd end up with if you used geoducks for pages. Now imagine flicking through one of those books, and getting the slimy geoduck residue on your hands as you look at the pages.
readingMnemonic: A page is a page ( ページ ). Hints Since the reading comes from the English word "page", this one shouldn't be too hard to remember, especially if you've already come across it in katakana.

meaningMnemonic: If you're stand ing under a tree and you see your parent , it's a good chance for a moment of intimacy . Hints Imagine yourself standing in the shade of a beautiful, big, old tree. You see your parent walk past and shout out to them. They come and join you, and it's like the two of you are the only two people in the world right now. That's intimacy.
readingMnemonic: Standing under the tree, you go to give your parent a big hug, but you manage to bang your shin ( しん )  on a huge tree root. Your parent pulls you in for a warm hug and rubs your shin. Despite the pain, it becomes an unforgettable "shin-timate" moment. Hints Busting your shins on things really hurts. I'm sure you've hit your shins on coffee tables and the like all your life. Remember that pain and think how much worse it would be banging your bare shins on pointy tree roots just when you were enjoying a moment of parental intimacy. Not enjoyable.

meaningMnemonic: You have fins in private . But, you want the world to see them, so you take them public . Hints Picture yourself in private, with fins. You wish others could see them. "That's it," you decide. "It's time to show the world. I'm going to make my fins public!"
readingMnemonic: You head out into the public where everyone can see your fins, but... things have changed. All people are the same. There are thousands of こう いち s walking around, and they all stare at you (though they pretend like they aren't). Hints How long have you been hiding in private with your fins? The public areas have changed, and all the people have become こういち s. One mother こういち --pushing a baby こういち --looks up and stares at your fins. Now you remember why you never go out in public.

meaningMnemonic: You have to say what you’re sell ing because people don’t like to read . If they walk right by and don’t read, you better say what you have for sale so they’ll know! Read it out loud to them. Hints Imagine reading what you have for sale out loud to people walking by because they’re too lazy to read it for themselves.
readingMnemonic: What are you forced to read aloud to sell? Yo- yo ( よ ) instructions! You’d think they’d be self explanatory, but there are actually a lot of rules and tricks that you have to read to get good at yo-yoing. Read all of these out loud so you can sell them. Hints Imagine reading through your list of yo-yo tricks. Do you know how to pronounce those weird yo-yo names?

meaningMnemonic: Look at the ground ! You spilled some water drop s, so I request that you wipe them up. I'd do it myself, but you're the one who spilled them, so I'm requesting that you do it. Pretty reasonable request, right? Hints It's a simple request, really. Just wipe up those water drops off the ground.
readingMnemonic: Oh, one more thing. I request that you wipe up the water with this cu cumber ( きゅう ). Hints "But cucumbers are already mostly water, this isn't going to absorb anything!" you cry. Well, too bad. That's my request, so you better do it. Figure out how to make the cucumber work.

meaningMnemonic: If your car runs into a cloud you'll revolve around it instead of going straight through. Clouds are really hard to see through, so even though you're trying not to, you revolve in a tight circle up and around the cloud anyway. Hints Imagine driving your car around and around the cloud, instead of going through it. At least it's soft and cool.
readingMnemonic: You have to revolve around the cloud ten ( てん ) times before it disappears and you're able to go through. Hints Unfortunately, not long after you get through that cloud another one comes down and gets in your way. Now you're counting each revolution, one... two... three... all the way up to ten.

meaningMnemonic: If you've been walking all day, your foot is the last thing anyone would want to kiss , especially after wandering barefoot down a road . Your feet are filthy, sweaty, and stinky. Nobody is going to want to kiss those feet. Hints Imagine kissing someone's foot. Now imagine kissing someone's foot after they've been walking down a road for hours. It's disgusting. Smell the stench of sweat wafting up into your nostrils as the foot approaches your lips. It's wretched.
readingMnemonic: What was this person walking down again? Oh, that's right – a ro ad ( ろ ). They were walking down a filthy road. Hints Walking down a road barefoot like this is a sure way to dirty up your feet. Feel the dirt, rocks, and twigs under your feet. The road is hard and dry and is not making your journey very comfortable at all.

meaningMnemonic: A sick stick of dynamite is going to be sick forever. Unfortunately there are no medicines that are effective on sticks of dynamite, so once they contract a sickness, they’re sick for good. Hints Imagine if you were a sick stick of dynamite. Every time you sneezed you ran the risk of blowing up. It would be a terrifying way to live. Just imagine it.
readingMnemonic: Being nervous all the time about spontaneously exploding would probably make you sweat profusely. And you know what sweating causes? B.O. ( びょう ). You’d be one smelly stick of dynamite. B.O. is a very unpleasant smell, and being sick is no excuse. Hints Picture this as your life. You could explode at any moment, you’re sick, and you have B.O. Nobody wants to be around you because you might explode and kill them, and you stink. What a terrible way to live!

meaningMnemonic: The tree marked with a yellow X on the side of the house is going to get cut down. You’ve marked it with a yellow X so the hired help knows which tree to cut down. There are a lot of trees on the side of the house, but the tree marked with a yellow X is the only one in danger of causing damage to your roof in the event of a storm. Hints Picture the scene of a woman with a chainsaw cutting down this tree marked with a yellow X. Hear the sound of the chainsaw buzzing and the grinding of wood as it meets the side of the trunk. It’s very loud. Woodchips go flying everywhere.
readingMnemonic: Wait, that woman with the chainsaw is Yoko ( よこ ) Ono! Yes, the same Yoko Ono who’s married to John Lennon of the Beatles. What’s she doing chopping down trees on the side of your house? Who can say. Silly Yoko. Hints Now picture the same scene as before only imagining Yoko Ono wielding that chainsaw. Maybe she’s dancing. Maybe there’s some Beatles music playing in the background. Either way it’s a strange sight – remember it.

meaningMnemonic: Angle your sword correctly at this cow to solve its riddle. The key is to untie the cow with the sword without hurting it. Hints Will you be able to solve this cow riddle? Picture yourself carefully trying to untie a cow with a sword at just the right angle. What a tricky thing to solve.
readingMnemonic: Did I mention that you have to solve this whole riddle while on a kay ak ( かい )? No?! Whoops. Hints So you're on a kayak, with a cow, and you have to find just the right angle with your sword in order to untie the cow and solve this riddle. A bit much to wrap one's head around. Anyway, good luck with that.

meaningMnemonic: If a lip ring (or two in this case) is what you lack , it's going to be way easier for you to sing a song . Hints Imagine singing a song with a couple lip rings in your mouth. The articulation will be all wrong! It's definitely better to lack lip rings if you're going to sing.
readingMnemonic: Where are you always singing song s, by the way? In your ca r ( か ). It's not just you, either. Pretty much everyone likes to sing in their car. Hints There's something about your car that makes your singing sound so much better than usual, you know?

meaningMnemonic: This kanji is the same as the radical — straight as straight can be. It can also mean direct , because when you go straight to a place, you're going there directly. Depending on the context it can even mean fix , since fixing something means straightening out all the messed up crooked bits. Hints Here's some straight talk for ya: if you study your radicals, you'll have no problem with this one.
readingMnemonic: Put food straight into your esophagus without chewing and you will choke ( ちょく ). You want to get straight to the most important part of eating — the digesting part — but if you don't follow all the intermediate steps, you'll end up choking. Hints Imagine shoving food straight down your esophagus and choking as you do. Why would you do this to yourself?!

meaningMnemonic: A good leader can put the ground 's history to great use . You are a good leader. You have studied the ground and dirt of the earth your entire life. You know the history of the ground and you know how to use it. Hints Smell the ground. Waft the earthy smell of history into your leader-like nostrils. What does it smell like? It smells useful. And also like ground.
readingMnemonic: You use the ground to raise shee p ( し ). When you were down there sniffing around you realized that your people will flourish best if you use this land for grazing and raising sheep. Hints When you use the ground for sheep like this, your people rejoice. You're the best leader ever! You always use everything to your advantage!

meaningMnemonic: Run into oneself in a dream and you'll definitely wake up . Hints If you run into yourself, it really messes you up, you know? You won't be able to handle what you're seeing so you have to wake up.
readingMnemonic: If one runs into oneself and you don't wake up , just look down at your waist. If you're wearing an o bi ( お ) you know it's a dream and you'll eventually wake up. If you aren't wearing an obi then it isn't a dream and you don't have anything to wake up from. Hints Your obi is like a special object you only have in dreams. If you have your obi, it's okay, it's a dream and you can wake up now! Make sure you memorize exactly how it feels so dream-you can't trick you or something.

meaningMnemonic: Your study history ? There must be a more educated way of putting this… Ah, yes, it's your academic history . You know, like the high school and university you graduated from — your educational background . Very important stuff in Japan.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: inferiority complex about one's educational background
academic background filter, educational background screening
to ask about someone's academic history
to have an education, to have academic credentials

sentences.japanese: それ、学歴サギですよね？
学歴がないのがコンプレックスなんです。
sentences.english: I have an inferiority complex about my lack of education.

sentences.japanese: 私の父にとっては、学歴が全てなんです。
sentences.english: For my father, one's academic background is everything.

sentences.japanese: 学歴はふつうだけど、ワニカニ歴は長いですよ。
sentences.english: My academic history is ordinary, but my WaniKani history is long.

meaningMnemonic: A study institution is an academy . That's where all the fancy people study, anyways.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 私はトーフグ学院で心理学を学んでいます。
sentences.english: I am studying psychology at Tofugu Institute.

sentences.japanese: 友人は、2014年に文化学院に入学しました。
sentences.english: My friend entered the Bunka Gakuin in 2014.

sentences.japanese: 学院では主に科学と数学の科目を教えています。
sentences.english: The academy mainly teaches science and mathematics.

sentences.japanese: 青山学院大学は東京にある大学の名前です。
sentences.english: Aoyama Gakuin University is the name of a university in Tokyo.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how 足す means "to add?" Add calculate to that and you'll have addition ! It's the type of calculation you're doing when you add.
readingMnemonic: This is the kun'yomi reading for 足 and the on'yomi for 算 . And the さん reading is rendaku'd into ざん . This is the same for all the math-ish words (addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division), so try to remember that, because you'll see it again!

sentences.japanese: 私の兄は、足し算が上手で早いです。
sentences.english: My brother is good and fast at adding.

sentences.japanese: この足し算の答えは正しくありません。
sentences.english: The answer to this addition is incorrect.

sentences.japanese: 次回の数学のクラスで足し算のテストがあります。
sentences.english: There will be a test for additions in the next math class.

meaningMnemonic: When something advance s and go es, it is moving forward. So this means advance or progress . 進行 can be used to describe various situations, like when a project progresses; but also when an illness advances to a more serious stage.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 道の工事が進行しています。
sentences.english: The construction of the road is progressing.

sentences.japanese: 先日、プロジェクトの進行ステータスをリポートしました。
sentences.english: The other day, I reported on the progress status of the project.

sentences.japanese: フグのエキスから作られた新しいワクチンが病気の進行を止めました。
sentences.english: The new vaccine made from blowfish extract has suppressed the progression of the disease.

meaningMnemonic: What's another way to call the farming business ? If you encapsulated it into one word (assuming we're talking about plant farming, here), you could call it agriculture .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 私たちの町では、米の農業をしてる人々が多いです。
sentences.english: In our town, there are many people who are farming rice.

sentences.japanese: 農業はハードワークですが、国民の生活にとって大切です。
sentences.english: Agriculture is hard work, but it is important for people's lives.

sentences.japanese: アイルランドから、日本の農業の文化を学びに来ました。
sentences.english: I came from Ireland to learn about the culture of Japanese agriculture.

sentences.japanese: 今、バイオダイナミックという農業の方法が人気です。
sentences.english: The agriculture method called Biodynamics is popular now.

meaningMnemonic: You chort le ( ちょっと ) a little at a silly joke. You can’t help chortling for a moment . Go ahead, chortle just a little, for just a moment, to help you remember this word.

sentences.japanese: ちょっとちがう気がする。
sentences.english: I think it's a little different.

sentences.japanese: ちょっと考えてみるよ。
sentences.english: I'll think about it a little.

meaningMnemonic: If you think about it, an earth road isn't going to be the main road. It will be the road less traveled. You could call it a path (you know, like a dirt path!) or a dirt road . Alternatively, another less traveled street that would probably be made out of dirt back in the day (before everything was paved) would be an alley . Imagine yourself walking down a dirt alley at night with no shoes. Scary!
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You've learned these readings already, so you should be able to read this word too! And remember, that it's the じ reading that you learned with 生地 here.

sentences.japanese: 下町の路地には、たくさんのネコが住んでいます。
sentences.english: Many cats live in the alley of the downtown area.

sentences.japanese: その魚屋は、西通りから少し路地に入った所にあります。
sentences.english: The fish store is in an alley just off of Western Street.

sentences.japanese: この辺の路地、夜に歩く時は、安全に気を付けてね。
sentences.english: Be careful for your safety when you walk in an alley around here at night.

meaningMnemonic: Something that is tall in degree s can either refer to its altitude , or to the fact that it's quite high-level . Note that this can refer to any altitude, even lower ones. But when used to refer to, for example, skills or a technique, it always talks about a high level or degree.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: このUFOは、今、高度3万3000フィートのところにいる。
sentences.english: This UFO is now at an altitude of 33,000 feet.

sentences.japanese: マイケルは、高度なテクニックで、むずかしいゲームを次々クリアした。
sentences.english: Michael completed one difficult game after another with advanced techniques.

sentences.japanese: 高度が一気に上ると、エンジンが止まっちゃうんだよ。
sentences.english: When the altitude gets too high, the engine will suddenly stop.

meaningMnemonic: What would heaven use to send messages and interact with us? An angel . Angels are always being used by the heavenly powers to run errands, deliver messages, and smite a bad guy or two.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 子犬は天使みたいでした。
sentences.english: The puppy was like an angel.

sentences.japanese: コウイチ君は、天使のようなスマイルがチャームポイントです。
sentences.english: What's charming about Koichi is his angelic smile.

sentences.japanese: 本当に、あなた天使なんですか？
天使は毎週やって来た。ただし来るのはゴミの日だけだった。
sentences.english: The angel came every week. But only on garbage day.

meaningMnemonic: You know 回 means "times," but it can also mean "revolve." You revolve around an answer until you're ready to give your answer or response to the question! 回答 refers to responding to a question, inquiry, or request. For example, you use 回答 when answering a questionnaire or letting someone know whether you can attend a party.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You didn't learn the on'yomi for 答 with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Give me your answer and I'll take you to とう きょう . How does that sound? All I need is your reply, and we'll be in とうきょう before you know it.

sentences.japanese: こちらに回答を入力してください。
アンケートへのご回答、ありがとうございました。
sentences.english: Thank you for your response to the survey.

sentences.japanese: 社長はインタビューを受ける事について、まだ回答を出していない。
sentences.english: The president has not yet responded about accepting an interview or not.

meaningMnemonic: What is it called when you calculate numbers ? That is the study of math and arithmetic .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 算数の先生は、田中先生です。
sentences.english: The teacher of arithmetic is Tanaka-sensei.

sentences.japanese: 明日の算数のクラスに必要な道具は全部持ったの？
sentences.english: Do you have all the tools you need for tomorrow's arithmetic class?

sentences.japanese: 算数のテストで答えが分からない時は、とりあえず一か四と答えておけば平気です。
sentences.english: If you don't know the answer on the arithmetic test, you can just say one or four and it'll be just fine.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how 手 can mean a "doer" in some words? What do you think your help doer is? It’s someone who helps you, so it’s your assistant , helper , or aide .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You learned the on'yomi reading of 手 with the vocabulary word 投手 .

sentences.japanese: 弟は心理学者の助手です。
sentences.english: My brother is an assistant of a psychologist.

sentences.japanese: 私の助手は三人の子の母でもあります。
sentences.english: My assistant is also the mother of three children.

sentences.japanese: 社長の助手として、コーヒーを買ってきたり、電話に出たりします。
sentences.english: As the president's assistant, I do things like getting coffee and answering the phone for them.

sentences.japanese: 仮に私が首になった助手の助手だとしたら、それってつまり私も首になっちゃったってこと？
sentences.english: If I'm the assistant to an assistant who was just fired, does that mean that I’m fired too?

meaningMnemonic: Doing something both fast and early probably requires you to do it at once or immediately . Whatever it is, be sure to do it without delay .
readingMnemonic: The reading for this one is strange. The reading for 速 ( そく ) is what you'd expect (on'yomi), but 早 gets a reading you haven't seen before, meaning you should treat this as an exception. Just think about how you're learning this word at once and without delay so there's no time for any sa ss ( さっ ), just kanji learning.

sentences.japanese: 早速、新しいアプリをダウンロードしました。
sentences.english: I immediately downloaded a new app.

sentences.japanese: 早速のお返事、どうもありがとうございます。
sentences.english: Thank you very much for your prompt reply.

sentences.japanese: 自立してから早速、自分の車を自分のお金で買いました。
sentences.english: Immediately after becoming independent, I bought my own car with my own money.

meaningMnemonic: When you distribute your heart around you, it's like your heart is everywhere at once, but not in your body. You feel frantic, you don't know what to do because your heart is out there. This represents the feeling you have when you have a worry or concern . 心配しないでね！
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Take note that the ぱい in 配 got rendaku'd from はい , as well.

sentences.japanese: 心配しないで、平気ですよ。全て上手くいくはず。
sentences.english: Don't worry, it's okay. Everything should work out.

sentences.japanese: 明日の試験が心配で、安心していられません。
sentences.english: I'm so worried about tomorrow's exam that I can't feel at ease.

sentences.japanese: 父にいつもの元気がないので、少し心配です。
sentences.english: I'm a little worried because my father doesn't have the energy like he always had.

sentences.japanese: この船の進行方向が西なのか東なのか分からなくて心配になった。
sentences.english: I was worried because I could not tell whether the ship was heading east or west.

meaningMnemonic: A self revolving car . You'd think this would be a regular car, but bicycles were probably introduced before cars were, meaning the self revolving car is the bicycle, not the car. Just imagine yourself on a bike, and you don't even have to move the pedals. They revolve themselves, but now you're going too fast and it's scary.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: to go out on a bicycle
to be able to ride a bicycle

sentences.japanese: すみません。この辺に自転車のパーキングはありますか？
sentences.english: Excuse me. Is there bicycle parking around here?

sentences.japanese: 私は毎日自転車でパン作り教室に通っています。
sentences.english: I go to the baking workshop every day by bicycle.

sentences.japanese: 自転車を買ってあげるよ。お返しは要らないからね！
sentences.english: I'll buy you a new bicycle. I don't need anything in return!

meaningMnemonic: The kanji for 苦 means suffering . This word, however, is a bit different, but you'll see how it's related. It means bitter tasting . Think of putting the most bitter thing in the world in your mouth. You feel sick, your mouth gets all weird, and you try to spit it out but the bitterness remains. Obviously eating bitter tasting things will cause you to suffer.
readingMnemonic: This reading of the kanji is unique to this meaning of the word, so here's a mnemonic to help you out! The taste is so bitter tasting that you fall to your knees really, really hard. Luckily, you were wearing your knee gua rds ( にが ). Feel the relief that you were wearing them. Ack, no relief now. It's still bitter in your mouth.

sentences.japanese: 父は苦いコーヒーを気に入ってます。
苦いフルーツなんて、この世の中に有るんですか？
sentences.english: Is there a bitter fruit in this world?

sentences.japanese: カラメルは、こがさないように気を付けてください。でないと、苦い味になってしまいます。
sentences.english: Be careful not to let the caramel burn or it will taste bitter.

meaningMnemonic: パン is the katakana version of the Portuguese word "pão" and means bread in English. If you know the Portuguese, Spanish, or French word for bread, you shouldn't have trouble remembering this word. If not, here's a mnemonic to help you: You use a pan ( パン ) to make all your bread . It's your special bread pan, and all the bread you make with it is delicious.

sentences.japanese: 朝はいつもパンを食べます。
sentences.english: I always eat bread in the mornings.
It says bread crusts are 100 yen.

meaningMnemonic: ビル is the Japanese version of the English word building . It usually refers to buildings that are taller than they are wide, most commonly apartment blocks and office buildings.

sentences.english: the building in which the head office is located
buildings are visible, can see buildings

sentences.japanese: うちの会社は、あそこのオフィスビルに入ってるんだよ。
sentences.english: My company is in that office building over there.

sentences.japanese: ビルから出たら、電話するよ。
sentences.english: I'll call you when I get out of the building.

sentences.japanese: ビルの谷間に月が見えた。
sentences.english: The moon was visible in a gap between the tall buildings.

meaningMnemonic: There is only one place in Japan that has a thousand leaves and that's Chiba . Picture all of those leaves swirling around you on your vacation to Chiba. Beautiful.
readingMnemonic: This is a place name and it uses the kun'yomi. You haven't learned kun'yomi for 千 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it: While you're admiring all of the leaves in Chiba , you realize you're craving something. What goes well with watching leaves? Why, chee se ( ち ) of course. Delicious Chiba cheese. Oh, and also note the rendaku on 葉 — it changes from は to ば .

sentences.japanese: 東京ディズニーリゾートは、千葉県にあります。
sentences.english: Tokyo Disney Resort is located in Chiba Prefecture.

sentences.japanese: 千葉から東京まで電車で行くと、大体四十分かかります。
sentences.english: It takes about forty minutes by train to go from Chiba to Tokyo.

sentences.japanese: 千葉のピーナッツは、家の中で対立が生まれるほど、おいしいんです。
sentences.english: Peanuts from Chiba are so delicious that it creates conflict at home.

meaningMnemonic: A friend who is like one of your parent s is someone who will look out for you. They are like family, in fact! That's why this word means best friend or close friend . Just imagine someone who watches over you like a parent would. This is the way to describe them.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: the figure of one's close friend
to say to a close friend

sentences.japanese: 親友の考えに反対した。
sentences.english: I opposed my best friend's thoughts.

sentences.japanese: 私たちって、友人以上、親友以下よね。
sentences.english: We are more than friends but less than best friends, don't you think?

sentences.japanese: レイチェルとは去年の夏に出会って、すぐに親友になりました。
sentences.english: I met Rachel last summer and soon became best friends with her.

sentences.japanese: 親友のバースデープレゼントに一頭のラマをあげようと思ってるんです。
sentences.english: I'm thinking of giving my best friend a llama as a birthday present.

meaningMnemonic: When you collect gold you are collecting money (or doing money collection ). Of course, back in the day gold was like money, which is why this word works the way it does. Hopefully you don't have to deal with too much 集金 in your daily life. We'll try to keep WaniKani nice and reasonably priced for you. 集金 often refers to collecting bills, dues, or fees in person or through a designated representative. This can be carried out by a business, an organization, or even just a small group of people.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: Today is the day of money collection.

sentences.japanese: もしもし、集金のお知らせでお電話しました。
sentences.english: Hello, I'm calling to notify you for the collection of money.

sentences.japanese: 先日、集金に行ったら、お客さんのお金が足りなかったので、代わりに玉ねぎを二つもらってきました。
sentences.english: When I went to collect money the other day, the client didn't have enough money, so I got two onions instead.

meaningMnemonic: When you collect to the middle of yourself, you are collecting towards your brain. All energy is going towards there, massing up in the middle, giving you extreme concentration and focus .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: to plan a focus, to plan a consolidation

sentences.japanese: 試験の間は、集中しましょう。
パパがゲームに集中している時は、話しかけない方がいいよ。
sentences.english: You should not talk to Dad when he is concentrated in a game.

sentences.japanese: ミーティングに集中しすぎて、朝ごはんをまだ食べてないことを今思い出しました。
sentences.english: I was too focused on the meeting that I've just remembered that I haven't had my breakfast yet.

sentences.japanese: 日本は、東京などの大きな町に人口が集中しています。
sentences.english: In Japan, the population is concentrated in large cities such as Tokyo.

meaningMnemonic: Imagine yourself investigating a child . You heard this child was having a rough time, so you need to come check on the condition of his home and life. readingMnemonic: The reading for the kanji in this vocab is the same as the one you learned with the kanji, meaning you should be able to read this.

sentences.english: We were lucky as there were no deaths or injuries from this typhoon.

meaningMnemonic: You've hopefully seen 向く and 向ける by now. They mean "to face" and "to turn toward." This has a similar idea. When you add 向け to something imagine you're turning it, aiming it at someone. It's aimed at them, meaning it's made for them. Turn a book toward someone, now it's aimed at them, it's made for them. See the connection?
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the word 向く so work off of that word to be able to read this one.
